questiontext.text: Which pair of operations does a Fenwick tree (Binary Indexed Tree) support in O(log n)?

answer.text: Prefix-sum query and point update

feedback.text: Correct — a BIT computes prefix sums and applies point updates, each in O(log n).

answer.text: Find minimum and delete minimum

feedback.text: Those are heap operations, not a Fenwick tree's role.

answer.text: Insert key and search key in sorted order

feedback.text: That describes a search tree.

answer.text: Union and find of set representatives

feedback.text: Those are disjoint-set operations.

generalfeedback.text: A Fenwick tree supports prefix-sum queries and point updates in O(log n) using the binary representation of indices.

questiontext.text: How does a Fenwick tree move between the indices it must touch during a query or update?

answer.text: By jumping via the lowest set bit, computed as i & -i (the "lowbit")

feedback.text: Correct — adding or subtracting i & -i walks the responsibility ranges.

answer.text: By following left and right child pointers of a binary tree

feedback.text: A BIT stores no explicit child pointers; it uses index arithmetic.

answer.text: By binary searching the array each step

feedback.text: No search is needed; the lowbit gives the next index directly.

answer.text: By hashing the index into a bucket

feedback.text: No hashing is involved; it is pure bit manipulation.

generalfeedback.text: The lowbit i & -i isolates the least-significant set bit; adding it (update) or subtracting it (query) steps through O(log n) indices.

questiontext.text: How much space does a Fenwick tree use for n elements?

answer.text: O(n) — a single array of size about n, with a small constant

feedback.text: Correct — a BIT is just one array, lighter than a segment tree.

answer.text: O(n log n)

feedback.text: A Fenwick tree is only O(n); each index owns exactly one range.

answer.text: O(log n)

feedback.text: You still need one slot per element, so space is O(n).
Far too much; a BIT is linear in space.

generalfeedback.text: A Fenwick tree needs just one array of size ~n (O(n) space) with a small constant — simpler and lighter than a segment tree.

questiontext.text: Compared with a segment tree, what is a key limitation of a plain Fenwick tree?

answer.text: It is less general — best for invertible/prefix aggregates like sums; range-minimum is not directly supported

feedback.text: Correct — subtraction of prefixes needs invertibility, so range-min does not map onto a plain BIT.

answer.text: It uses more memory than a segment tree

feedback.text: The opposite — a BIT is lighter, using a single O(n) array.

answer.text: Its queries are O(n) instead of O(log n)

feedback.text: No — BIT queries are O(log n).

answer.text: It cannot perform point updates

feedback.text: Point updates are one of its two core operations.

generalfeedback.text: A Fenwick tree is simpler and lighter than a segment tree but less general: it shines for invertible/prefix aggregates (sums), whereas range-min/max are not directly supported.

questiontext.text: Which statements about Fenwick trees (BITs) are true? (select all that apply)

answer.text: Prefix-sum queries and point updates both run in O(log n)

feedback.text: Yes — each touches O(log n) indices.

answer.text: It uses only O(n) space with a small constant factor

feedback.text: Yes — a single array, lighter than a segment tree.

answer.text: It naturally supports range-minimum queries like a segment tree

feedback.text: No — range-min is not invertible, so a plain BIT cannot do it directly.

answer.text: It keeps its elements sorted for binary search

feedback.text: No — a BIT indexes by position and does not sort values.

generalfeedback.text: A BIT gives O(log n) prefix sums and point updates in O(n) space via lowbit index arithmetic; it is less general than a segment tree and does not do range-min.

questiontext.text: The value i & -i that isolates the least-significant set bit of an index is commonly called the ______.

answer.text: lowbit

feedback.text: Correct — the lowbit, i & -i.
